title: MATH GAOKAO - 20
description: Authentic-style mathematics problems inspired by China’s Gaokao — build deeper understanding, sharper thinking, and real exam readiness.

questions.learningObjective: Translate the phrase “at least” into an inequality.
questions.question: The phrase “\(x\) is at least \(5\)” translates mathematically to which statement?
questions.explanation:
The phrase “at least \(5\)” means that \(5\) is the minimum allowed value of \(x\). Therefore, \(x\) can be equal to \(5\) or greater than \(5\). In mathematical notation, this is written as
\[
x\ge 5.
\]
Option A, \(x\le 5\), means “at most \(5\),” which is the opposite condition.
questions.hint: The phrase “at least” includes equality and allows larger values.

questions.learningObjective: Translate the phrase “at most” into an inequality.
questions.question: The phrase “\(x\) is at most \(7\)” translates mathematically to which statement?
questions.explanation:
The phrase “at most \(7\)” means that \(7\) is the maximum allowed value of \(x\). Therefore, \(x\) can be equal to \(7\) or less than \(7\). In mathematical notation, this is written as
\[
x\le 7.
\]
Option A, \(x\ge 7\), means “at least \(7\),” which is the opposite condition.
questions.hint: The phrase “at most” includes equality and allows smaller values.

questions.learningObjective: Translate the phrase “not more than” into an inequality.
questions.question: The phrase “\(x\) is not more than \(10\)” translates mathematically to which statement?
questions.explanation:
The phrase “not more than \(10\)” means that \(x\) cannot exceed \(10\), but it may equal \(10\). Therefore, the correct inequality is
\[
x\le 10.
\]
Option B, \(x<10\), excludes the value \(10\), so it does not fully capture “not more than \(10\).”
questions.hint: “Not more than” is equivalent to “at most,” which includes equality.

questions.question: The phrase “\(y\) exceeds \(x\) by \(3\)” translates mathematically to which equation?
questions.explanation:
“\(y\) exceeds \(x\) by \(3\)” means that \(y\) is \(3\) more than \(x\). Therefore,
\[
y=x+3.
\]
Option A, \(y+3=x\), would mean \(y=x-3\), which says that \(y\) is \(3\) less than \(x\), not greater by \(3\).
questions.hint: “Exceeds by \(3\)” means the first quantity is larger by \(3\).

questions.learningObjective: Translate a verbal statement about a sum and reciprocal into an inequality.
questions.question: For a positive real number \(x\), the phrase “the sum of \(x\) and its reciprocal is at least \(2\)” translates mathematically to which statement?
questions.explanation:
The phrase “at least \(2\)” means the quantity is greater than or equal to \(2\). The sum of \(x\) and its reciprocal is
\[
x+\frac{1}{x}.
\]
Thus the statement translates to
\[
x+\frac{1}{x}\ge 2.
\]
Option B, \(x+\frac{1}{x}>2\), excludes the possibility of equality. When \(x=1\), we have \(1+\frac{1}{1}=2\), so equality does occur.
questions.hint: “At least” means greater than or equal to, so equality must be included.

questions.learningObjective: Translate “the product is negative” into an inequality.
questions.question: The phrase “the product of \(x\) and \(y\) is negative” translates mathematically to which statement?
questions.explanation:
The product of \(x\) and \(y\) is written \(xy\). Saying the product is negative means
\[
xy<0.
\]
Option A, \(x+y<0\), concerns the sum, not the product, so it is not the correct translation.

questions.learningObjective: Translate “there exists” into an existential quantifier.
questions.question: The phrase “there exists a real number whose square is \(2\)” translates mathematically to which statement?
questions.explanation:
The phrase “there exists” indicates an existential quantifier, written \(\exists\). The property is that the square of the number is \(2\). Therefore, the statement translates to
\[
\exists x\in\mathbb{R},\,x^2=2.
\]
Option B uses the universal quantifier \(\forall\), meaning every real number has square \(2\), which is false and not the intended translation.

questions.learningObjective: Translate a verbal universal statement into quantifier notation.
questions.question: The phrase “every integer greater than \(1\) has a prime divisor” translates mathematically to which statement?

options.label: A
options.text: \(\forall n\in\mathbb{Z},\,\bigl(n>1\implies \exists p,\,(p\text{ is prime}\land p\mid n)\bigr)\)

options.label: B
options.text: \(\exists n\in\mathbb{Z},\,\bigl(n>1\land \forall p,\,(p\text{ is prime}\implies p\nmid n)\bigr)\)

questions.explanation:
The phrase begins with “every integer greater than \(1\),” which is a universal statement over integers with the condition \(n>1\). The property is that the integer has a prime divisor, meaning there exists a prime \(p\) such that \(p\mid n\). Therefore, the correct translation is
\[
\forall n\in\mathbb{Z},\,\bigl(n>1\implies \exists p,\,(p\text{ is prime}\land p\mid n)\bigr).
\]
Option B is an existential statement saying that some integer greater than \(1\) has no prime divisor, which is a different statement.
questions.hint: “Every integer greater than \(1\)” becomes a universal quantifier with an implication \(n>1\implies\cdots\).

questions.learningObjective: Translate “between inclusive” into a compound inequality.
questions.question: The phrase “\(x\) is between \(-2\) and \(3\), inclusive” translates mathematically to which statement?
questions.explanation:
The word “inclusive” means that the endpoints \(-2\) and \(3\) are included. Therefore, the compound inequality must use \(\le\) on both sides:
\[
-2\le x\le 3.
\]
Option A, \(-2<x<3\), excludes both endpoints, so it does not match “inclusive.”
questions.hint: “Inclusive” means the endpoints are allowed, so use \(\le\), not \(<\).

questions.learningObjective: Translate the formal definition of a limit into quantifier notation.
questions.question: The phrase “for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(\delta>0\) such that, for every \(x\) in the domain of \(f\), if \(0<|x-a|<\delta\), then \(|f(x)-L|<\varepsilon\)” translates mathematically to which statement?
questions.explanation:
The quantifiers must remain in the order “for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists \(\delta>0\), for every \(x\) in the domain of \(f\).” The antecedent must use the punctured neighborhood \(0<|x-a|<\delta\), because the value at \(x=a\) is irrelevant to the limit. Thus the correct translation is
\[
\forall \varepsilon>0,\,\exists \delta>0,\,\forall x\in\operatorname{dom}(f),\,\bigl(0<|x-a|<\delta\implies |f(x)-L|<\varepsilon\bigr).
\]
Option B is the negation of this statement, not its translation.
questions.hint: Preserve the quantifier order and include the punctured-neighborhood condition \(0<|x-a|<\delta\).
